_comment: Single source of truth for Talon's blog. Edit this file, then run: python tools/build-blog.py && python tools/build-sitemap.py. Never hand-edit anything under /journal/ - the builder overwrites it. Adding a post is an entry in `posts` below; nothing else needs touching.

_field_guide.slug: URL segment. Lowercase, hyphens, no dates. Becomes /journal/<slug>/ and cannot be changed later without breaking links.
_field_guide.title: The headline, as published. Used as the <h1> and in the <title> tag.
_field_guide.date: YYYY-MM-DD. Drives ordering and the published date shown on the page.
_field_guide.date_source: Where the date came from. Say plainly if it is an authoring date rather than a confirmed publication date - this bit Hollie's site once.
_field_guide.tag: One of the values in `tags` below. Shown on the card and used by the archive filter.
_field_guide.area: Optional. A service area from `service_areas` below, when a post is genuinely about that place. Drives the local-SEO half of the blog. Leave empty for general posts - do NOT tag a post with an area it is not really about.
_field_guide.excerpt: 1-2 sentences for the archive card and the meta description. Written, not auto-truncated.
_field_guide.paragraphs: Array of strings, one per paragraph. Plain text; the builder escapes and wraps them.
_field_guide.image: Card image, 3:2, ~800px. Empty string renders the branded placeholder instead.
_field_guide.image_wide: Post banner, 2:1, ~1440px. Empty string renders the placeholder.
_field_guide.image_alt: Describe what the image SHOWS, including any words lettered inside it. Empty alt is only for decoration.
_field_guide.eyebrow: Optional. Overrides the tag as the category label shown above the H1 and as the trailing breadcrumb crumb. Use when a post's filter tag (kept short/reused) shouldn't be the same string as its displayed category, e.g. tag "Planning & Budget" but eyebrow "Planning & Preconstruction". Falls back to `tag` when absent.
_field_guide.deck: Optional. A one-to-two sentence subheading rendered in italic directly under the H1. Supports the same inline **bold**/[link](url) as paragraphs. Leave out for a post that doesn't need one - most won't.
_field_guide.short_answer: Optional. A concise 2-3 sentence answer rendered in a visually set-apart callout right after the hero image, before the body. Written for both a skimming reader and an AI answer engine. Leave out unless the post genuinely reduces to one clean answer.
_field_guide.cta_heading: Optional. Overrides the default 'Thinking about a project?' CTA heading at the foot of the post.
_field_guide.cta_body: Optional. Overrides the default CTA paragraph.
_field_guide.cta_href: Optional. Overrides the default CTA link target (/#contact).
_field_guide.cta_label: Optional. Overrides the default CTA button label ('Start Your Project').

_service_areas_note: From the live GBP service-area list, confirmed 2026-09-01. The site currently names only Penn Valley, Lake Wildwood, Nevada County and the Sierra Foothills - the rest have no on-site presence at all, which is the local-SEO gap the blog is partly here to close. Do not invent an area that is not on this list.
_tags_note: Keep this list short. Every tag becomes a filter button on the archive, and a filter with one post in it is worse than no filter.
_posts_note: EMPTY ON PURPOSE. The pipeline was built 2026-09-08 ahead of Kim supplying the articles. With no posts, /journal renders an honest empty state rather than a broken page, and it is NOT linked from the site nav or the sitemap until at least one post exists - see build-blog.py.

posts.title: Welcome to The Journal
posts.date_source: Authoring date, not a confirmed publication date. Update this to the day it actually goes live.
posts.excerpt: Talon Construction Company is starting to write down the answers we give homeowners every week — what a foothill build actually involves, where budgets go wrong, and what we ran into on real projects.
paragraphs: Most of what we know about building in Nevada County was learned on job sites, not in a classroom — on foothill lots, since 1981. This is where we are going to start writing some of it down.

Homeowners ask us the same questions before a project starts. What will this actually cost? How long will it take? Why does that slope change the foundation? Do I need a permit for this? What happens if we find something once the walls are open? Those are good questions, and they deserve better than a rushed answer over the phone.
## What is The Journal?

**The Journal** is Talon Construction Company's working notebook, published. It is where we answer the questions homeowners actually ask us, one at a time, in enough detail to be useful before you have hired anybody.

It is not a news feed and it is not a portfolio. If we do not have something useful to say about a subject, we will wait until we do. A post here should either save you a phone call or tell you what to ask on the next one.
## What will we write about?
Three things, in roughly equal measure.

- **Building in the foothills.** Slopes, access, drainage, lake-area requirements, aging structures, and the weather that shapes all of it — the conditions that make a Nevada County build different from a build on flat ground.
- **Planning and budget.** The part of a project most likely to go wrong, and the easiest to get right early. Scope, allowances, unknowns, and where the money actually goes.
- **The work itself.** What we are building, what we ran into, and how it was solved. Specific projects rather than general advice.
Where a post is about a real project, we will say which one and what the conditions were. A claim about how something performs is worth reading only if you can tell where it came from.
## Who is writing this?

Talon is three people. Jordon O'Hara works in the field, on building knowledge and day-to-day leadership on site. Mike Novo founded the company and holds the license. Erik Oxenbol works on management, and how a project gets organized and run from start to finish. All three work to the standards Mike set, and you will see all three names in what gets written here.

**Talon Construction Company** is a California licensed general contractor working out of Penn Valley. Michael Novo has personally held license CSLB #397350 since January 1981 — not the company, him, for forty-five years.
That license carries four classifications:
- **Class A**, General Engineering Contractor
- **Class B**, General Building Contractor
- **C-12**, Earthwork and Paving Contractors
- **C-42**, Sanitation System Contractor

Together those cover site engineering, the building itself, earthwork and septic. That is close to the range a foothill project tends to ask for. You can check any California contractor's license yourself, including ours, on the [CSLB license lookup](https://www.cslb.ca.gov/onlineservices/checklicenseII/checklicense.aspx). We would rather you did.
## Where does Talon work?

Talon works across Nevada County and into the surrounding foothills: Penn Valley, Lake Wildwood, Lake of the Pines, Grass Valley, Nevada City, Rough and Ready, North San Juan, Colfax, Truckee and Tahoe City.

Those places do not build the same way. A lake-area remodel answers to rules a Grass Valley addition never sees. Truckee carries a snow load and a season that closes early. Where a post applies to one of them in particular, we will say so rather than leave you to guess.
## What should we write about?

If there is something you would like us to cover, call us at (530) 432-3633 or send it through the contact form. A question you have not been able to get a straight answer to is exactly the kind we want. That is a genuine offer — the best posts here will come from questions homeowners actually asked.
The standard we try to hold to here is the same one we bring to a job. Say what is true, explain the decisions, and do not promise what cannot be delivered.

posts.title: Before We Build Your Home, We Build It on Paper
posts.date_source: Date from Kim's original draft spec, prepared 2026-09-14. Confirm this is meant to be the published date, or update to the actual go-live date if it differs.
posts.deck: A detailed proposal doesn't just show you a price — it shows you whether the builder actually understands your project. Here's how Talon builds every custom home on paper before anyone breaks ground.
posts.excerpt: A custom home proposal should do more than show a price. See how Talon uses detailed preconstruction planning to understand a project before building begins.
posts.short_answer: A detailed custom home proposal should explain the scope of work, major construction phases and how the proposed cost relates to the work being performed. At Talon, the proposal also becomes part of the roadmap used to manage the project after construction begins.
paragraphs: A detailed construction proposal should do more than tell you what a project costs. It should show you that the builder understands what they are being asked to build.

At Talon Construction Company, preparing a proposal for a custom home or major remodel can take days. We study the architectural plans, think through how the work will actually be performed, and break the project down phase by phase and task by task.
That level of detail is intentional. We build the project on paper before we build it in the field.
## A proposal is part of the construction process
It is easy to think of a proposal as the document that comes before the real work begins. We see it differently. For Talon, preparing the proposal is one of the first stages of the work itself.

We look at the drawings from the perspective of the people who will eventually have to execute them. That means considering the sequence of construction, the work our own crew will perform, where specialty trades will be involved, and how one phase needs to come together before the next can begin.

Then we document it. The result is not simply a few broad categories with a total at the bottom. It is a detailed outline of how we understand the project and what we believe it will take to build it properly.
## Detail creates clarity before construction begins
Custom homes contain thousands of decisions. Some are large and obvious. Others are buried inside the work and may never be visible to the homeowner once construction is complete.

The more clearly a project can be defined before work begins, the better everyone understands what has been proposed. The homeowner can see what is included. The Talon team knows what has been committed to. Trade partners understand where their work fits into the larger project. And when construction begins, there is already a structure to work from.

That doesn't mean every possible condition can be predicted. Construction doesn't work that way. It means we've taken the time to understand as much as reasonably possible before asking a client to commit.
## The proposal becomes a roadmap

One of the biggest benefits of preparing a project this way is that the proposal doesn't become irrelevant once it is accepted. Much of the organization established during estimating becomes the framework for managing the project.

The work has already been considered in phases. Tasks have been identified. Responsibilities have been considered. The sequence has begun to take shape. That gives the homeowner and the Talon team a common reference point as construction progresses.
For a substantial custom home or remodel, that matters. There are simply too many moving parts to manage well from memory, assumptions or a handful of broad line items.

It takes time. We think it should. Talon may spend days developing a proposal for a project we ultimately never build. That's part of the business. We're not interested in producing an artificially fast proposal simply to get a number in front of a prospective client. If we're going to tell someone what we believe their project will cost and how we intend to approach it, we want to have done the work behind that answer.

And for a homeowner comparing builders, the proposal can tell you something important before construction ever begins. Ask one simple question: **Does this proposal show that the builder understands my project?**
Not just the square footage. Not just the finishes. The project.
## What should you look for in a construction proposal?
More pages do not automatically make a proposal better. Detail only matters when it creates understanding. A useful proposal should help you determine:
- What work is actually included?
- How has the builder organized the project?
- Are the major phases understandable?
- Can you see how the proposed price relates to the work?
- Can the builder clearly explain the proposal when you have questions?
- Does it appear that someone has genuinely studied your plans?
If the last answer is no, the number at the bottom of the page may not tell you as much as you think.
## Good construction starts before the jobsite
The visible part of building comes later. The framing. The concrete. The cabinetry. The finishes.
Before any of that happens, there is planning. For Talon, that planning begins when we receive the drawings and start working through the project one piece at a time.
It's detailed work, and most of it isn't particularly glamorous. But it creates something we value highly: clarity. And clarity is a very good place to start a custom home.
